title: Documents close: the Church writes letters
hook: the Church still writes to the world, as Paul wrote to churches
tomorrow: a king says, you fed me. when did they ever see him hungry?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a title in the past tense: he loved us, a love already given that nothing can take back.

Group projects have a typist. One person at the keyboard, everyone else talking over their shoulder. Near the end of Paul's letter to the Romans, the typist speaks up. In the Douay-Rheims: "I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord." Paul talked, Tertius wrote, and the letter went off to people with names in a city far away. This whole block has read the Church's documents. At the close, a question worth arguing: who are those documents actually for?
screen: `THE ONE AT THE KEYBOARD.` → `I TERTIUS, WHO WROTE THIS.` → `WHO ARE THEY FOR?`

segments.voice: There are two honest answers, and both have a case. One side says: leave them to people trained to read them. They come in different weights: a council's constitution, a pope's encyclical, an exhortation. Read one paragraph alone and it's easy to make it say what you wanted. The Church gives bishops, priests and teachers to read them with you, and that's a gift, not a gate. The other side says: they're letters, so open them. Paul tells the Colossians that once his letter has been read among them, they should have it read in the church at Laodicea too. Read aloud, passed on. And Laudato Si' says outright it's written to every person on the planet. Hear this block with both voices in mind. Numbered paragraphs, so a whole Church can land on the same line. The Council: God speaking to us as friends, the joys and hopes of the world taken as the Church's own, no coercion in faith, one human family. Then the popes: witnesses first, the person as the way, put out into the deep, an encounter, hope that changes life, a Church bruised from the street, time greater than space, everything connected, the woman at the market, Christ alive, he loved us. Different authors, different weights. One shape. Each was written to someone, and a letter isn't finished when it's sealed. It waits for an answer.
screen: `LEAVE THEM TO THE TRAINED.` · `THEY'RE LETTERS: OPEN THEM.` · `READ AT LAODICEA TOO.` · `DIFFERENT WEIGHTS, ONE SHAPE.` · then, large: `STILL WRITING.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper. Choose one person you'd write to about what you hold most dear: a child, a friend, your younger self. Write only the first sentence, by hand, and let it sit there unfinished.
Documents close. The end of this block of Church documents, read as letters: written to someone, passed on, waiting for an answer.
Your line: still writing. The documents end here, and tomorrow the works of mercy begin. That's the block.

howItsDone: Church documents are read in parishes, schools and study groups, often a few numbered paragraphs at a time, and quoted in homilies so whole communities hear the same lines.

chat.says: english essay: write a letter that matters. dad says pick one person, not 'the world.' why?
options: Letters live by being read by someone real. Paul wrote to people with names; it got passed on from there.
Because letters to the world are against the rules; only popes are allowed to write those.
Because one person is easier to grade. A letter's audience doesn't really change anything.
chat.meaning: Paul wrote to real people, and his letters were read aloud and passed on. A letter is written to someone and waits for an answer.

Tertius.meaning: the man who wrote down Paul's letter to the Romans

epistle.meaning: an old word for a letter, used for Paul's

Laodicea.meaning: an ancient city near Colossae with a church Paul wrote to

Colossians.meaning: the church in Colossae; Paul's letter to them

encyclical.meaning: a pope's formal teaching letter to the Church
